title: Case study: Shoprite, a transnational corporation and its global links

blocks.heading: The case study: a real transnational corporation
blocks.text: A required case study of one real transnational corporation and its global links: Shoprite Holdings, the South African food retail group - what it is, where it operates, and how its links join Namibia to the wider region and beyond.

blocks.heading: The corporation and its scale
blocks.text: Shoprite Holdings is a transnational corporation: a company that operates in more than one country. It grew from a Cape Town supermarket chain founded in 1979 into Africa's largest food retailer, with its head office at Brackenfell in Cape Town and a listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. By the 2020s it ran more than 3 000 stores in about 15 African countries (approximate figures), selling groceries to millions of shoppers a week. Namibia was its first step outside South Africa, in 1990, and the group now trades from more than 30 Namibian towns, from Windhoek to Katima Mulilo. That spread makes it a textbook example: one head office, many countries, and a web of links between them.

blocks.heading: Its global links, followed one by one
blocks.text: Each link has a direction, and naming it is what the case study asks for. Goods: fresh produce and packaged stock are sourced from farms and factories in several countries and move through the group's large distribution centres in South Africa before reaching Namibian shelves, though stores also buy from Namibian bakers, dairies and vegetable growers. People: Namibian staff work in the stores of a company whose buying, pricing and strategy are decided at the Cape Town head office. Money: the prices Namibian shoppers pay flow back partly as wages and local supplier payments, and partly as profit to the group's shareholders. So a single tin on a Windhoek shelf joins Namibia to farms, factories, workers and investors in several countries at once - which is globalisation, drawn at the scale of one shop.

blocks.heading: Why there, or what there?
blocks.text: A frequent error in questions about transnational corporations is describing what the company does in a place - the jobs it creates, the wages it pays - when the question asks why it operates there. Location reasons (the market, lower labour costs, transport links, government incentives) are not the same as impacts (jobs, wages, pollution, profits leaving the country). The test is whether the answer says why the company is there, or what it does there.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The case study ties the globalisation process of topic 3.1 to the industrial location factors of topic 3.3 and to the urban employment of topics 1.6 and 1.7, and its packaged-goods trade links to the food systems of topic 3.2.
